_about: Spoken lines for the recorded demo. Keys are the walkthrough screenshot ids (the video holds on each one long enough to say its line), plus '<part>:intro' (title card) and '<part>:signin:<role>'. Edit a line, re-run record_demo.py and build_narration.py: the pause follows the length of the line.
2d:intro: Next is the Monitoring Sheet. This is the curriculum grid the Graduate School used to keep in Excel: one row per student, one column per subject. In the portal, staff keep this record up to date on the screen itself, and every entry remembers where it came from.
2d:signin:Graduate School Staff: I sign in as Graduate School staff.
monitoring-sheet-01: This is the Monitoring Sheet, under Records. I pick the Master of Science in Nursing program. Each row is a student and each column is a subject in the curriculum; the colour shows whether the subject is completed, enrolled, or not yet taken. The legend explains every mark, and staff can still upload a workbook under Student Handoff if they prefer.
monitoring-sheet-02: Let's add a student who is not in the imported sheet yet. The window says up front that this is recorded as a manual entry, with my name and the time.
monitoring-sheet-03: I type the student ID, the first and last name, and the school year of entry. The same required fields and duplicate checks as the workbook import apply here, so a manual entry cannot be sloppier than an import.
monitoring-sheet-04: The student is added, and a Student Portal login is created for them, exactly like the import would do. Now I add their subjects right away.
monitoring-sheet-05: This is the student's record panel. It lists all eighteen subjects of the curriculum, all not taken yet, with the units counted for us.
monitoring-sheet-06: I add a subject row: status Completed, the term it was taken, and a remark, here 'credited from a transfer record'.
monitoring-sheet-07: After the second subject, the panel shows two of eighteen completed and six units. Notice the Source column: both rows are marked Manual entry, so nobody will mistake them for imported data.
monitoring-sheet-08: If a remark needs correcting, I edit the row. Because this row was entered in the portal, a simple edit is enough.
monitoring-sheet-09: Removing a row is different: the system asks for a reason, and it explains that the row is not erased. It goes back to not taken and stays in the history.
monitoring-sheet-10: One completed subject remains, and the counts update immediately.
monitoring-sheet-11: This is the Change history tab. Every add, change and removal is listed with the old value, the new value, who did it, when, the source, and the reason. This is the audit trail the Graduate School can rely on.
monitoring-sheet-12: Back on the grid, the new student carries a Manual tag, and the cell entered by hand has a small orange dot, so manual data is visible at a glance.
monitoring-sheet-13: Now an imported student, Katrina Cabrera. Here every row says Imported: these values came from the official workbook.
monitoring-sheet-14: If I try to change an imported value, the system requires a reason before it will save, and that reason goes into the history with my name. Official values are never overwritten silently. And grades are never entered here: AIMS stays the official source for grades.
2h-1:intro: Now Leave of Absence, Readmission and AWOL. These three run on the same kind of board, so once you have seen one, you know all of them. First, a student asks for a leave.
2h-1:signin:Student: I sign in as Daniel Fernandez, a Master of Arts in Education student who has accepted a work assignment in another city.
leave-of-absence-01: Under Requests, he opens Leave of Absence. The form tells him the limits straight away: up to two semesters at a time, renewable once, and never more than four semesters in total.
leave-of-absence-02: He can open 'Rules applied on this screen'. These are the same rules the staff will apply, each with its Handbook page. The ones marked Needs review are prototype values the Graduate School still has to confirm.
leave-of-absence-03: He chooses when the leave starts and ends, the system tells him that is two semesters, and he gives the reason and a short explanation.
leave-of-absence-04: Before anything is sent, he sees a summary to check: from, to, and the reason.
leave-of-absence-05: It is submitted. He can see the tracker: staff review, Dean decision, the leave begins, and his return. He always knows who has his request right now.
2h-1:signin:Graduate School Staff: Now the Graduate School staff side.
leave-of-absence-06: This is the Leave of Absence board. Each column is a stage, and each card is a request. I search for Daniel: his card is in Submitted, flagged 'awaiting your review'.
leave-of-absence-07: I drag the card to In staff review. Dragging does exactly the same as the buttons, and the server still checks every move, so a card cannot be dragged somewhere the rules do not allow.
leave-of-absence-08: The same requests can be read as a table, if staff prefer a list.
leave-of-absence-09: I open the request. It shows the leave period, the reason, and what the student wrote.
leave-of-absence-10: Below that is the policy check, advice for staff. Each rule shows Pass or Needs review. Minimum residency says Needs review because it is a prototype rule. The check never decides: the Dean does.
leave-of-absence-11: I forward it to the Dean with a note explaining what I checked.
leave-of-absence-12: The card moves to With the Dean and is locked for staff. The board says 'Waiting for: Dean' instead of hiding the card.
2h-1:signin:Dean: Now I sign in as the Dean.
leave-of-absence-13: The Dean sees the same board, with the requests waiting for a decision.
leave-of-absence-14: The Dean drags the card to Leave scheduled. The approval window opens, and the Dean can add a note the student will read.
leave-of-absence-15: Approved. The card is in Leave scheduled and is flagged for the Registrar. The Dean could also have returned it for revision or denied it, both with a comment.
leave-of-absence-16: Back as staff, the card waits in Leave scheduled. Normally the leave starts by itself on its first day.
leave-of-absence-17: For the demonstration, I start the leave now by dragging the card to On leave.
leave-of-absence-18: Daniel is now on leave, and enrollment is closed for him while he is away.
leave-of-absence-19: Further down is the Registrar list. The portal sends no e-mail: staff download the list, send it through the official channel, then mark it sent and later acknowledged.
leave-of-absence-20: I download the list. The system reminds me that no e-mail was sent by the portal.
leave-of-absence-21: I tick Daniel and mark the list as sent to the Registrar, so the office always knows what was handed over and what was not.
leave-of-absence-22: And on the student's side, Daniel sees that he is on leave, with every message he received along the way.
2h-2:intro: That was leaving properly. Readmission is the other end: coming back from an approved leave.
2h-2:signin:Student: I sign in as Therese Lacson, who is already on an approved leave.
readmission-01: Her Readmission page says she is on leave and that enrollment stays closed until a readmission is approved. The leave she is ending is filled in for her.
readmission-02: The rule behind this page: a returning student writes an intent to enroll, from the Handbook, page fifty-three.
readmission-03: She picks the semester she wants to return in, explains why she is ready, and confirms the four checklist items.
readmission-04: Again, a summary to check before sending.
readmission-05: Submitted, with a four-step tracker: staff review, Dean decision, and back in the program.
readmission-06: The Readmission board: the same board, with its own columns. Therese's card is in Submitted.
readmission-07: I drag it to In staff review.
readmission-08: The request shows the return semester, her intention, and the linked leave of absence.
readmission-09: The return checklist shows what the student ticked, not yet verified by staff. Below, her history: one year in the program and two of four leave semesters already used.
readmission-10: The policy check flags one thing: she wants to return before her leave ends. That is allowed only if the Dean agrees, so it says Needs review.
readmission-11: When I forward, I tick the checklist items I verified myself. Anything I leave unticked reaches the Dean as Needs review.
readmission-12: Forwarded, and locked: waiting for the Dean.
readmission-13: The Dean finds Therese's request in With the Dean.
readmission-14: The Dean drags it to Approved, back in the program, with a note.
readmission-15: She is active again. Note that readmission restores her standing; it does not enroll her in subjects. That is the Academic Coordinator's next step.
readmission-16: On the staff board, the card now says the next owner is the Academic Coordinator, and it is flagged for the Registrar.
readmission-17: The Registrar list works exactly as before: download, send it yourself, mark sent, mark acknowledged.
readmission-18: And Therese sees her readmission approved, with the messages from staff and the Dean.
2h-3:intro: The last one is the improper way out: a student who stopped enrolling without an approved leave. Nobody types 'AWOL' by hand. The system flags the student from the official records.
awol-01: This is the AWOL and Residency board. It flags cases from the source records, and the line above counts the cases in each column.
awol-02: I search for Maya Torres. Her card is in the AWOL column, AWOL since July fifth, and it says 'Waiting for: Student'. Staff cannot move it: only the student can start a return.
awol-03: The rules here are the residence limits: five years normal and seven absolute for a master's student, seven and nine for a doctorate, and time on leave counts toward residence. Each rule shows its Handbook page.
awol-04: Opening the card shows the AWOL date, where the flag came from, and the last enrolled semester. There is no button for staff yet.
2h-3:signin:Student: Now I sign in as Maya.
awol-05: Her Return from AWOL page shows the flag, and a note that registration stays restricted until her return is reviewed.
awol-06: She chooses her intended return semester and her last enrolled semester, and writes her intention and her reason for returning.
awol-07: She checks the summary and sends it.
awol-08: Submitted. The system classifies her as within the maximum residence, and she cannot cancel it herself; she has to contact the Graduate School office.
awol-09: Back on the staff board, the card has moved by itself to Return review.
awol-10: The request shows her written intention, the residence limits, and the policy check: eligible for Dean review.
awol-11: I drag it to With the Dean and add a note.
awol-13: The Dean finds Maya's card in With the Dean.
awol-14: The Dean drags it to Back in the program. The window explains that approval restores her standing.
awol-15: The card lands in Back in the program: she is active again.
awol-16: On the staff side, the next owner is the Academic Coordinator, because enrollment is a separate step.
awol-17: All four steps of the tracker are complete.
awol-18: The Registrar list here is a list of reports, one per approved return. Staff download it and send it through the official channel.
awol-19: And Maya sees her return approved. So leave, return and AWOL all ran on the same board, the same request window and the same Registrar list.
2l:intro: Every case so far followed one student. Reports and Analytics answer the other question: what does the Graduate School know about all of its students at once? Every number here is computed from the records, not typed in.
2l:signin:Graduate School Staff: I sign in as Graduate School staff.
reports-tour-01: Reports and Analytics is under Overview. At the top are three filters: program, entry cohort, and the period, which by default is the last twelve months. Below them is a strip of six numbers that answer the questions the office asks most often.
reports-tour-02: For example, Behind schedule: the share of active students who are behind, compared with a target, so you can see at once whether the Graduate School is on track.
reports-tour-03: Median days to decide shows how quickly requests are decided, compared with the twelve months before. Every number comes from recorded events, so it changes as the work is done.
reports-tour-04: The first tab, Needs attention, asks: what is holding students back? Each bar is a cause, and the longest bar affects the most students.
reports-tour-05: Selecting a cause narrows the list below to the students it affects, so the bar is never just a number.
reports-tour-06: Show all causes brings back the full list: most delayed first, with the stage, the main reason, the days in that stage, and the office that can move the student on. It downloads as Excel or PDF with the same filters.
reports-tour-07: Where students get stuck shows, for each lifecycle stage, how many students are on time, slow, or stuck, with the limits written underneath.
reports-tour-08: Office speed shows which offices take longest to close requests, grouped by how many days they have been waiting. The longest red bar is the office to ask first.
reports-tour-09: Records to fix lists research students with missing records, for example no adviser on file. Once the record is fixed, the student leaves the list.
reports-tour-10: The detailed lists are still here. Cohorts by stage shows how many students of each program and entry year are at each stage.
reports-tour-11: Graduation candidates shows who can graduate, what is still missing, and where each student stands in a graduation batch.
reports-tour-12: Overdue and pending lists every task and request still waiting, longest wait first, with the office that must act.
reports-tour-13: Defenses lists the defenses held and upcoming, with the panel and the verdict.
reports-tour-14: Registrar changes is the daily list of changes made here that the Registrar must apply in AIMS, each one marked when it is sent.
reports-tour-15: And every filter applies to everything on the page. Here I choose one program, and all six numbers and the charts follow. This is how the Graduate School can monitor many students at once, instead of checking records one by one.
reports-tour-07b: Every count on these screens is a button. Selecting one opens the real students behind it, with a link to each record, so nobody has to take a figure on trust.
